items.title: Headlines for November 20, 2026 | Democracy Now!
items.excerpt: ## Senate Rejects War Powers Resolution to Limit Trump’s Attacks on Iran Nov 20, 2026 The Senate rejected a war powers resolution on Thursday that would have directed President Trump to seek congressional approval before resuming attacks on Iran. The resolution failed on a vote of 51-48. Three Republicans voted in favor, while Pennsylvania Democratic Senator John Fetterman voted in opposition. The House approved the resolution in September. Both the House and Senate previously approved a war powers resolution back in June, but President Trump largely ignored it. Thursday’s failed vote in the Senate came after Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries suggested he would not block funding for attacks on Iran in the government funding package due by December 11. Meanwhile, a Pentagon official said Thursday the cost of the war on Iran has topped $48 billion. That figure does not include damage to U.S. bases, the cost of providing healthcare to hundreds of injured troops or the tens of billions of dollars in higher fuel costs triggered by the war. ## Senate Passes Permitting Reform Bill with Support of 14 Democrats, Including Leader Chuck Schumer Nov 20, 2026 The Senate has approved a permitting reform bill that would weaken environmental laws to speed approval of new housing, roads, energy projects and other infrastructure. While the bill would make it easier to build new transmission lines and wind and solar farms, it would also speed construction of fossil fuel power plants and new data centers, including on public lands. Meanwhile, Native leaders and advocacy groups strongly opposed the legislation, saying it would weaken tribal sovereignty and threaten cultural and sacred sites. This is Oregon Democratic Senator Jeff Merkley, who voted “no.” ... Despite those objections, the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as BAAJA, passed on a vote of 62-33 with 14 Democrats in favor, including Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer. In a ... The bill now goes to the House and is expected to be voted on the week after next. ## Climate Activists Condemn “Slimmed-Down” COP31 Draft Text That Makes No Reference to Fossil Fuels Nov 20, 2026 Here at the COP31 U.N. climate summit, negotiators published a “slimmed-down” draft text on Thursday that stripped out any reference to fossil fuels, or ending their use. Instead, the document promotes carbon capture and storage, an unproven technology that critics say will never have a meaningful impact on the climate crisis. Activists at the COP are demanding more financing to help poorer countries adapt to a warming world. This is Iona Stewart of the climate action group Global Witness. ... ## Russian Attacks Kill 8 After Ukraine Bombs Bridge Connecting Russia to Occupied Crimea Nov 20, 2026 In Ukraine, officials say eight people were killed and dozens injured overnight, as Russia launched a massive drone and missile attack. In Kyiv, Russian bombs struck three ⁠bridges over the Dnipro River. Meanwhile, in Kharkiv, a Russian drone damaged a hospital, wounding four people. The Russian attacks came after Ukraine bombed the Kerch Bridge, the only link between mainland Russia and Russian-annexed Crimea. Engineers say it could take years for Russia to repair the damage. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky defended the bridge strike and warned of further action.

items.title: Bessent advocates lower Fed rate hike, cites energy shock By Reuters
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON, Nov 20 (Reuters) - US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent urged the Federal Reserve to not embrace a big interest rate hike as some Fed governors are doing, citing the energy supply shock and a drop in crude delivery prices. Bessent said in an interview with CNBC that one governor who is backing 50 basis point hike had wanted a similar cut within the last year. "So it seems somewhat peripatetic to now want a the bigger hike just 12 months or 11 months later," he said. "So I would encourage the Fed to look forward, not backwards."

items.title: ’Black Friday’ brings consumer spending into focus for AI-rocked market By Reuters
items.excerpt: NEW YORK, Nov 20 (Reuters) - Investors will turn attention next week to the strength of consumer spending, as they hope evidence of a broadly solid economic backdrop can provide stability for a US stock market that has been shaken by unease about the AI trade. Next week, "Black Friday" heralds the onrush of the holiday shopping season as retailers offer a wave of discounts. Investors will watch for signs of how consumers are coping with inflation, including rising energy and borrowing costs. Consumer spending accounts for roughly two-thirds of the US economy. ... Weakness in stocks could threaten consumers’ holiday gift-buying, if they feel less wealthy and less likely to spend. Oxford Economics estimates that holiday retail sales will rise 4.2%, or an increase of 2.2% in volume after adjusting for inflation. That covers retail spending in November and December, excluding autos, gasoline, and bars and restaurants. The National Retail Federation projects 182.7 million consumers plan to shop this year during the five-day Thanksgiving period that runs to "Cyber Monday", citing results from a recent survey. Black Friday is expected to be the most popular day to shop during that period. That overall number would be down slightly from 186.9 million last year, but continues the trend of elevated shopping during the holiday weekend in recent years, the NRF said. Government data this week showed US retail sales for October increased moderately, while the core measure of such sales rose faster than expected. Retailers including Walmart and Target had upbeat comments or outlooks for the holiday season in their quarterly reports this week. "The consumer is pretty healthy, and we’d like to see that continue through the end of the year," Nolte said. COULD GASOLINE PRICES SAP SHOPPING? Despite solid retail sales data, Gene Goldman, chief investment officer at Cetera Financial Group, said he was worried "that the consumer is being impacted by higher gas prices, higher energy prices, higher food prices." The average national price for a gallon of gasoline stood on Thursday at $3.72, according to motorists’ group AAA. That is down from nearly $4.30 a month ago, but well above the $3.09 level a year ago. As the holiday shopping season heats up, Goldman said he was watching the extent of shopping done in stores compared to online, and how much consumers are buying necessities versus discretionary items.

items.title: Oil prices set for third straight weekly decline on Middle East export flows
items.excerpt: Oil prices rose on Friday but were set for a weekly decline as concerns over supply disruptions grew following Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia's capital Riyadh and reports of tanker disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. ... Brent ​crude futures were down $1.65, or 1.79%, to $90.33 a barrel at 1032 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate futures for December were down $1.62, or 1.95%, to $81.59 a barrel, while the more active January contract was down $1.22, or 1.48%, to $81.22. Brent is on track ⁠for ‌a 6% decline for the week and the December WTI contract ⁠for an 8% weekly drop as expectations of a supply surplus grew because crude shipments through the Strait of Hormuz have returned to roughly pre-war levels. This would be the benchmarks' third straight week of decline.

items.excerpt: ## Consumer sentiment reading moves higher as inflation outlook improves sharply ... The outlook for consumers improved in November as expectations for inflation eased, according to a University of Michigan survey Friday. The survey's headline sentiment index rose to 51.5, up 7.3% from a month ago and exactly in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate. Inflation expectations at the one-year horizon declined sharply, down to 3.7%, which was a full percentage point below a month ago and well below the mid-month November reading of 4.3%. This was the lowest reading since March. The five-year outlook slipped to 3.3%. "Despite the softening in inflation expectations, consumers continue to report overwhelmingly that inflation—rather than unemployment—will cause greater hardship for consumers in the next one or two years," survey director Joanne Hsu said.
